units.intro: This unit answers one huge question: *how is the information of life stored, copied, used, and passed on — and why do offspring resemble parents yet still differ?*

cards.title: 1.1 Nucleic acids · Let us discuss
paras: 4 questions to answer before you read on. Try each one, then open the answer.

questions.q: What are the four major macromolecules found in cells?
questions.a: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids.

questions.q: What is the function of nucleic acids?
questions.a: They store, copy and express genetic information; they direct protein synthesis.

questions.q: What are the building blocks of nucleic acids?
What is genetics?
questions.a: The study of heredity and hereditary variation.

cards.title: 1.1 Nucleic acids
body: Nucleic acids are long, thread-like informational molecules containing C, H, O, N and P. There are two types: **DNA** (deoxyribonucleic acid) and **RNA** (ribonucleic acid). They occur in all living cells and in viruses.

cards.title: The nucleotide — the building block
body: Each nucleotide has three parts:

- a five-carbon sugar (ribose in RNA, deoxyribose in DNA)
- a phosphate group
- a nitrogenous base
Sugar + base = **nucleoside**. Sugar + base + phosphate = **nucleotide**. Nucleotides join by phosphodiester bonds into a polynucleotide chain (sugar–phosphate backbone, bases sticking out).

cards.title: Nucleotide and polynucleotide
body: Figure N1. A nucleotide (left) and a short polynucleotide chain (right).

cards.title: The nucleotide — the building block
body: Bases: two **purines** (double ring) — adenine (A) and guanine (G); three **pyrimidines** (single ring) — cytosine (C), thymine (T, DNA only) and uracil (U, RNA only).

cards.title: Mnemonic — PURe As Gold
body: PURines = Adenine + Guanine (the bigger, 2-ring bases). Pyrimidines are the small ones: *CUT* the py (Cytosine, Uracil, Thymine).
**Pairing trick:** At The Grand Canyon — *A–T* and *G–C*. Weak couple A–T holds hands with 2 H-bonds; strong couple G–C with 3.
**RNA swap:** “Thymine Takes a bow, Uracil Usurps” — DNA has T, RNA has U.

cards.title: 1 · Sugar
body: DNA = *de*oxyribose (one oxygen missing). RNA = ribose. Think: DNA is the archive, so it is drier / more stable.

cards.title: 2 · Backbone
body: Sugar–phosphate–sugar–phosphate… Bases hang off like charms on a bracelet.

cards.title: 3 · Direction
body: Strands run antiparallel: 5′→3′ facing 3′→5′. Polymerases only add to the 3′ end.

cards.title: 1.1.1 DNA
body: DNA is the genetic material of prokaryotes, eukaryotes and many viruses. Genes are stretches of DNA that specify proteins. A DNA molecule is two complementary polynucleotide strands twisted into a **double helix**.

- Sides of the “ladder”: alternating deoxyribose and phosphate.
- Rungs: base pairs held by hydrogen bonds.
- **A pairs with T** (2 hydrogen bonds). **G pairs with C** (3 hydrogen bonds).

cards.title: Figure N2. Base pairing. The textbook draws this as a twisted ladder (double helix).
Do you know? (from the textbook)
body: The only difference between living organisms is the amount and order of the bases in their DNA. Each cell contains about 2.7 metres of DNA. In an average meal you eat roughly 55 million cells — about 149,128 km of DNA.

cards.title: Why DNA is an ideal genetic material
body:
- It stores information as a four-letter base sequence.
- It can replicate accurately (complementary pairing + proofreading).
- It is chemically more stable than RNA (deoxyribose; thymine instead of uracil).
- It can be expressed as proteins via RNA.

cards.title: 1.1.2 RNA
body: RNA is usually single-stranded, uses **ribose** and **uracil**, is shorter, and is less stable. Most RNA is in the cytoplasm. Three types:

cards.title: 1.1.2 RNA
head: Type
Role in the textbook’s three functions
rows: Carries instructions from nuclear DNA to ribosomes. Read in triplets called *codons*.
Picks up the correct amino acid and brings it to the ribosome. Has an *anticodon* complementary to the mRNA codon (AUG ↔ UAC).
Makes up the bulk / skeleton of the ribosome.

cards.title: 1.1.3 Protein synthesis — the central dogma
body: Textbook statement of the central dogma:
**DNA → (transcription) mRNA → (translation) protein**
and DNA also copies itself by **replication**.

cards.title: Figure N2b. Central dogma as a kitchen: recipe → copy → meal.
Mnemonic — Repli-TRANS-late
body: *Replication* = DNA to DNA (same language). *Transcription* = DNA to RNA (like transcribing notes into another notebook). *Translation* = RNA to protein (changing language: nucleotide → amino acid).
Codon vs anticodon: codon is ON the mRNA. Anticodon is ANTI (on tRNA), the opposite.

cards.title: A. Replication
body:
1. Starts at an **origin of replication** (many origins on a eukaryotic chromosome).
2. Hydrogen bonds break; strands separate.
3. **DNA polymerase** adds complementary nucleotides (A–T, G–C).
4. Each daughter DNA has one old strand and one new strand (semi-conservative — the idea implied by the textbook diagrams).
5. Polymerase proofreads mismatches.
Eukaryotic rate given in the book: 500–5000 base pairs per minute. A human cell copies ~6 billion base pairs in a few hours.

cards.title: Activity 1.2
paras: 1 question to answer before you read on. Try each one, then open the answer.

questions.q: How does DNA replication contribute to the continuity of life?
questions.a: Each daughter cell receives a complete, accurate copy of the parent’s genetic instructions, so growth, repair and asexual reproduction keep the same species identity from cell to cell and generation to generation.

cards.title: B. Transcription
body: RNA polymerase copies *one* DNA strand into mRNA in the nucleus.

1. DNA opens locally.
2. RNA nucleotides pair with the template (A–U, T–A, G–C, C–G).
3. A single RNA strand is released; DNA rewinds unchanged.

cards.title: Exam-safe wording
body: The textbook calls the transcribed DNA strand the “sense or coding strand”. In modern usage the *template* (antisense) strand is the one RNA polymerase reads; mRNA has the same sequence as the coding strand except U for T. Use the textbook wording in class, but understand the pairing.

cards.title: C. Translation (four textbook steps)
body:
1. **Ribosome assembly** — mRNA, tRNA and ribosomal parts meet in the cytoplasm.
2. **Initiation** — first tRNA binds the first codon; a second tRNA binds; a peptide bond forms (dipeptide).
3. **Elongation** — the ribosome moves codon by codon; the chain grows.
4. **Termination** — a stop codon is reached; the polypeptide is released.

cards.title: Worked example — complementary bases
body: DNA template: TAC GGA CAT ATT
mRNA: AUG CCU GUA UAA
tRNA anticodons: UAC GGA CAU AUU
Note: AUG is the usual start codon (methionine). UAA is a stop codon — translation ends here (Exercise 1.1 Q5).

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: Which of the following organic bases is a purine with a double-ring structure?

steps.text: **Given:** The list of organic nitrogenous bases.
**Formula/Rule:** Nitrogenous bases are categorized into two groups based on structure:
**Purines:** Double-ring structure, which includes Adenine ($$\text{A}$$) and Guanine ($$\text{G}$$).
**Pyrimidines:** Single-ring structure, which includes Cytosine ($$\text{C}$$), Thymine ($$\text{T}$$), and Uracil ($$\text{U}$$).
**Result:** Therefore, **Adenine** is the correct answer as it is a double-ringed purine.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: If a double-stranded DNA molecule contains $$30\%$$ Adenine, what is the percentage of Guanine?

steps.text: **Given:**
$$\text{Adenine (A)} = 30\%$$
**Formula:** According to Chargaff's rules:
$$\text{A} = \text{T}$$
$$\text{G} = \text{C}$$

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the correct complementary DNA strand for the sequence `5'-ATCGGCTA-3'`?
cards.why:
**Given:** DNA template sequence `5'-ATCGGCTA-3'`.

**Formula/Rule:** In DNA, base pairing rules dictate that:
- Adenine ($$\text{A}$$) pairs with Thymine ($$\text{T}$$)
- Cytosine ($$\text{C}$$) pairs with Guanine ($$\text{G}$$)
Additionally, DNA strands run antiparallel, meaning the complementary strand of a `5' \rightarrow 3'` sequence runs `3' \rightarrow 5'`.

**Substitution:**
- `A` at `5'`

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which molecule carries amino acids to the surface of ribosomes during translation?
cards.why:
**Given:** Functional roles of RNA types during translation.

**Formula/Rule:** 
- Messenger RNA ($$\text{mRNA}$$) carries the genetic blueprint from DNA.
- Ribosomal RNA ($$\text{rRNA}$$) forms the physical structure of ribosomes.
- Transfer RNA ($$\text{tRNA}$$) is responsible for matching codons and delivering specific amino acids.

**Result:** **tRNA** is the molecule that transfers amino acid

cards.title: 1.2 Cell division · Let us discuss
body:
1. How do organisms grow and reproduce?
2. Asexual vs sexual reproduction?
3. What is replication?
4. What are nucleic acids?

cards.title: 1.2 Cell division
body: **Cell division** = nuclear division + cytoplasmic division. The life of a cell from formation to next division is the **cell cycle**. The long preparation stage is **interphase**.

cards.title: Interphase (the textbook’s six points)
body:
1. Chromosomes are invisible threads of chromatin.
2. DNA replicates.
3. New organelles form.
4. In animal cells, centrioles replicate (plants have no centrioles).
5. Energy stores are built up.
6. Nuclear membrane and nucleolus remain intact.
After replication each chromosome = two sister **chromatids** joined by a **centromere**.

cards.title: 1.2.1 Mitosis and asexual reproduction
body: Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid body cells. Uses: growth, repair, replacement, asexual reproduction (especially in unicellular organisms).
**Karyokinesis** (nuclear division) has four stages, then **cytokinesis**.

cards.title: Prophase
body: Chromosomes condense as sister chromatids. Animal centrioles move to poles and form the spindle. Nuclear membrane and nucleolus break down.

cards.title: Metaphase
body: Chromosomes line up on the equator. Centromeres attach to spindle fibres.

cards.title: Anaphase
body: Centromeres split. Sister chromatids (now daughter chromosomes) are pulled to opposite poles.

cards.title: Telophase
body: Chromosomes arrive, uncoil; nuclear membrane and nucleolus reform; spindle disappears.

cards.title: 1.2.1 Mitosis and asexual reproduction
body: Cytokinesis: animals — cleavage furrow pinches the cell. Plants — a cell plate becomes a new cell wall.

cards.title: Mnemonic — PMAT
body: *Prophase* = Prepare (chromosomes appear, envelope vanishes). *Metaphase* = Middle (they line up). *Anaphase* = Apart (sisters separate). *Telophase* = Two nuclei (envelope returns).
Cytokinesis is the “C” after PMAT — Cutting the cytoplasm. Animal cell pinches like a belt; plant cell builds a wall like laying bricks.
**Meiosis extra:** “Meiosis I reduces, meiosis II resembles mitosis.” Crossing over = “swap shop in Prophase I.”

cards.title: Figure N3. Mitosis at a glance (compare textbook Figure 1.10 — plant vs animal).
1.2.2 Meiosis and sexual reproduction
body: Meiosis makes haploid gametes (sperm, eggs; also spores in plants). Two divisions: **meiosis I** (reduction division — homologues separate) and **meiosis II** (sister chromatids separate, mitosis-like). Result: four haploid cells that are genetically different because of **crossing over** and independent assortment.

**Prophase I** is the key difference: homologous chromosomes pair as **bivalents**. Chromatids may break and rejoin at **chiasmata** — **crossing over** swaps segments and creates new allele combinations.

- Metaphase I — bivalents at equator, homologues facing opposite poles.
- Anaphase I — homologues separate (centromeres do *not* split).
- Telophase I — two haploid cells.
- Meiosis II — like mitosis, producing four haploid cells (tetrad).
In humans: spermatogenesis yields four sperm; oogenesis yields one ovum and polar bodies (textbook Figure 1.12).

cards.title: 1.2.2 Meiosis and sexual reproduction
head: Mitosis
Meiosis
rows: No centromere split at anaphase I
Chiasmata and crossing over in prophase I

cards.title: 1.3 Genetics
body: **Genetics** is the study of heredity and variation. Two driving questions: why do offspring look like parents? Why do they also differ?
Human examples in the book: tongue rolling, free vs attached earlobes, hitchhiker’s thumb, widow’s peak, iris pigment, fingerprints, skin colour.

cards.title: 1.3.1 Mendel’s work
body: Gregor Johann Mendel (1822–1884), Austrian monk, used the garden pea *Pisum sativum*.
Why peas?

1. Grow quickly; one season to maturity.
2. Easy, controllable pollination (normally self-pollinating; can be cross-pollinated).
3. Fertile seeds after crossing.
4. Clear contrasting traits.

cards.title: 1.3.1 Mendel’s work
body: P / P₁ · parents · F₁ · first filial · F₂ · second filial · hybrid · offspring of different genotypes

**Genotype** = genetic constitution (TT, Tt, tt). **Phenotype** = appearance. **Homozygous** = identical alleles (TT or tt). **Heterozygous** = different alleles (Tt). **Allele** = alternative form of a gene.

cards.title: 1.3.2 Monohybrid crosses
body: One pair of contrasting traits. Cross TT (tall) × tt (dwarf) → all F₁ are Tt tall. Self the F₁:

cards.title: 1.3.2 Monohybrid crosses
body: Phenotypic ratio **3 : 1**. Genotypic ratio **1 : 2 : 1** (TT : Tt : tt). This is the monohybrid ratio Mendel found across all seven traits (Table 1.6 in the book).

cards.title: 3 tall : 1 dwarf
body: Cover one eye: you see tall, tall, tall, short. Recessive only wins as *tt*.

cards.title: 1 : 2 : 1 genotype
body: TT · Tt · Tt · tt — two of the four boxes are heterozygotes.

cards.title: Trick
body: If the numbers are “about half and half”, it was a test cross (Tt × tt), not an F₂.

cards.title: 1.3.3 Mendel’s laws
body: **Law of Dominance:** in a hybrid, the dominant character is expressed and the recessive remains hidden.
**Law of Segregation (and recombination):** the two factors (alleles) for a trait separate when gametes form; each gamete gets one; they recombine at fertilisation.

cards.title: 1.3.4 Test crosses
body: A tall plant may be TT or Tt. Cross it with homozygous recessive **tt**.

- If all offspring tall → unknown parent was TT.
- If 1 tall : 1 short → unknown parent was Tt.

cards.title: 1.3.5 Dihybrid crosses
body: Two traits at once. Round yellow (RRYY) × wrinkled green (rryy) → F₁ all RrYy (round yellow). F₂ phenotypic ratio **9 : 3 : 3 : 1**.
**Law of Independent Assortment:** allele pairs separate independently of other pairs during meiosis (true when genes are on different chromosomes).
F₁ gametes: RY, Ry, rY, ry. The 16-box Punnett square in textbook Figure 1.20 is the one you must be able to draw.

cards.title: Mnemonic — FOIL the heterozygote
body: For RrYy, list gametes with FOIL (First, Outer, Inner, Last): RY, Ry, rY, ry. Same four go across the top and down the side → 16 boxes.
**9:3:3:1 song:** “Nine both-dominant, three first-only, three second-only, one both-recessive.”
Independent assortment works when genes are on *different* chromosomes. If they travel together (linked), the ratio breaks.

cards.title: Worked dihybrid mini-count
body: Among 16 equally likely F₂ genotypes:

- 9 round yellow (at least one R and one Y)
- 3 round green (at least one R, yy)
- 3 wrinkled yellow (rr, at least one Y)
- 1 wrinkled green (rryy)

cards.title: 1.3.6 Incomplete dominance
body: Neither allele fully masks the other; heterozygote is intermediate. Classic textbook example: red × white four o’clock (or carnation) → all pink F₁. F₂ = 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white. Also reddish vs white coat in cattle and horses.

cards.title: 1.3.7 Multiple alleles — ABO blood groups
body: Three alleles: I^A, I^B, i (or I^O). Each person still has only two.

cards.title: 1.3.7 Multiple alleles — ABO blood groups
body: I^A and I^B are dominant to i. Uses: transfusion compatibility; supportive (not absolute) evidence in parentage disputes.

cards.title: Worked example (Activity 1.13 style)
body: Mother group A, father group B, child group O.
Child O must be **ii**, so each parent must have given *i*. Therefore mother is **I^Ai**, father is **I^Bi**.
Possible children of I^Ai × I^Bi: AB, A, B, O — each 1/4. Probability a second child is AB = **1/4** (independent of the first child).

cards.title: 1.3.8 Co-dominance
body: Both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygote. Textbook example: AB blood group — A and B antigens are both present. Contrast with incomplete dominance, where the heterozygote is a *blend* (pink), not both colours fully shown.

cards.title: Incomplete
body: Red + white = *pink*. Mix the paint. Ratio 1:2:1 phenotype.

cards.title: Co-dominance
body: A + B = *AB*. Both flags fly. Neither is watered down.

cards.title: ABO memory
body: O is “zero antigen” and recessive (i). A and B are the show-offs. Only ii = group O.

lessons.title: Sex Determination and Sex Linked Characters

cards.title: 1.4 Sex determination and sex-linked characters
body: Humans: 22 pairs of autosomes + 1 pair of sex chromosomes. Female **XX** (homogametic — all eggs carry X). Male **XY** (heterogametic — half the sperm carry X, half Y). The child’s sex is decided by whether the fertilising sperm brings X (girl) or Y (boy).

cards.title: 1.4 Sex determination and sex-linked characters
body: Expected ratio 1 female : 1 male.

cards.title: Mnemonic — Dad decides
body: Every egg is X. Sperm is X or Y. So the father determines sex. Boys show X-linked traits because they have “no spare X” — one bad allele and the trait appears. Girls need two copies.
Colour blindness / haemophilia: think “X marks the weak spot.”

cards.title: 1.4.1 Sex Determination
body: Sex is inherited by individuals in the same Mendelian fashion.
Sex determination in higher animals is controlled by a specific pair of chromosomes.
A karyotype is a display or photomicrograph of an individual’s body metaphase chromosomes that are arranged in a standard sequence.
The genes which control sexual development are located on sex chromosomes.

cards.title: 1.4.2 Sex-linked characters
body: Genes on the X chromosome (rarely Y) are sex-linked. They do not assort independently of sex. Because males have only one X, a single recessive allele on that X is expressed. That is why colour blindness and haemophilia are much more common in males.
Notation often used: X^HX^H normal female, X^HX^h carrier female, X^hX^h affected female; X^HY normal male, X^hY affected male.

cards.title: Example — colour-blind father, carrier-free mother
body: X^cY × X^CX^C → daughters all X^CX^c (carriers, normal vision); sons all X^CY (normal). A colour-blind son would need the allele from his mother.

cards.title: 1.4.2 Sex-Linked Characters
body: Sex-linked characters usually do not affect the females, only the males.
Colour Blindness: Colour blindness is the inability to distinguish the colours red and green (even brown, orange or yellow) by some people.
The identification of this disorder is important in modern life e.g. colour coding is often used in traffic lights.
Identify the visual capabilities of the offspring (progeny).

cards.title: 1.5 Mutation
body: A **mutation** is a sudden change in the amount or structure of DNA. Rare spontaneously; can be induced by **mutagens** — physical (X-rays, UV, gamma rays) or chemical (mustard gas, colchicine).
Often harmful (e.g. albinism — no melanin, sun-sensitive skin and eyes). Sometimes useful (insecticide resistance, antibiotic resistance in bacteria).

cards.title: 1.5.1 Chromosomal mutation (aberration)
body:
- **Deletion** — a segment is lost.
- **Duplication** — a segment is repeated.
- **Inversion** — a segment rotates 180° and reinserts.
- **Translocation** — a segment moves to a non-homologous chromosome.
- **Non-disjunction** — homologues or sister chromatids fail to separate in meiosis. Gametes get n+1 or n−1 chromosomes.

cards.title: Mnemonic — DDIT + N
body: Chromosome structure: *Deletion, Duplication, Inversion, Translocation*. Number: *Non-disjunction*.

Picture a necklace: lose a bead (deletion), copy a bead (duplication), flip a section (inversion), clip a piece onto another necklace (translocation), or the clasp fails to split the two strands (non-disjunction).

cards.title: 1.5.1 Chromosomal mutation (aberration)
body: **Down’s syndrome** (textbook): extra chromosome 21 (trisomy 21). Features listed: intellectual disability, slanting eyes, heart defects, thick tongue, short stature, stubby fingers.

cards.title: 1.5.2 Gene (point) mutation
body: Change of one or a few nucleotides, altering the amino-acid sequence of a protein.

- **Insertion** — extra base(s) added (often a frameshift).
- **Deletion** — base(s) removed (often a frameshift).
- **Substitution** — one base pair replaced by another.
- **Inversion** — a short run of bases reversed.

cards.title: What to ask next · Keep interrogating the book
body:
- If DNA polymerase makes a mistake that is not repaired, is that a gene mutation or a chromosomal mutation?
- Why does a frameshift insertion usually do more damage than a substitution?
- Can two group-O parents ever have an AB child? Why does that matter in court?
- If Lamarck were right, would the children of a weight-lifter be born more muscular?
- Why is energy lost between trophic levels, and how does that limit the length of food chains in an Eritrean grassland?
- Which abiotic factor most limits life in the Danakil / desert parts of Eritrea — and how are organisms adapted to it?

tips.text: DNA and RNA are two different nucleic acids found in the cells of every living organism. Both play a significant role in cell biology.
DNA and RNA are structurally similar because they both consist of long chains of nucleotide units. However, there are a few structural details that distinguish them from each other.
However, even with the differences in their structures, DNA and RNA have co-operating roles in the field of cell biology.
DNA contains the genetic information of an organism and this information dictates how the body’s cells will construct new proteins according to the organism’s genetic code.
DNA molecules duplicate themselves in a process known as replication.
DNA molecules control the synthesis of the proteins, which characterize each type of organism.
The structure of DNA directly controls the structure of proteins.
The message on DNA is changed to the message of proteins with the help of mRNA.
The formation of RNA from DNA is called transcription.
The mRNA then “escapes” from the nucleus to be translated into proteins by the process of translation.

units.title: Evolution
units.intro: Evolution, in this syllabus, is the idea that present-day complex organisms arose by gradual change from earlier, simpler forms over a very long time.

cards.title: 2.1 Theories of evolution · 2.1.1 Creationist and evolutionist views
body: Creationist accounts attribute the origin of life and of kinds of organisms to a Creator, typically as separate acts. Evolutionist accounts explain diversity by descent with modification. The textbook presents both as historical views that students should be able to describe.

cards.title: 2.1.2 Lamarck’s theory
body: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck proposed:

1. Use and disuse — organs used become stronger; unused organs waste away.
2. Inheritance of acquired characters — those changes are passed to offspring.

Classic story: giraffes stretching necks, offspring born with longer necks. This is rejected: acquired phenotypic changes (exercise, sun-tan, lost tail) are not written into gamete DNA and are not inherited.

cards.title: 2.1.3 Darwin’s theory of natural selection
body: Charles Darwin (voyage of HMS *Beagle*; Galápagos finches and tortoises; *On the Origin of Species*, 1859). Five points as in the book:

1. **Overproduction (fecundity)** — more offspring than can survive.
2. **Variation** — individuals of a species are not identical.
3. **Struggle for existence** — competition for food, space, water, mates.
4. **Survival of the fittest** — those whose variations fit the environment leave more offspring.
5. **Inheritance** — favourable variations are passed on; over generations they accumulate → new species.
**Artificial selection** (what breeders do with crops and livestock) was Darwin’s analogy for natural selection.

cards.title: Darwin's theory in five steps
body: Read the chain from top to bottom. Each step is one of the five points of Darwin’s theory in the textbook. Over many generations this leads to new varieties and species.

cards.title: Mnemonic — O.V.S.S.I.
body: *Overproduce · Vary · Struggle · Survive (the fit) · Inherit.*
Lamarck vs Darwin in one line: Lamarck said “need creates change, then kids inherit the gym muscles.” Darwin said “the already-better ones have more babies.”

cards.title: Homologous
body: Same plan, different job — human arm / bat wing / whale flipper. Common ancestor.

cards.title: Analogous
body: Same job, different plan — insect wing vs bird wing. Same problem, separate solutions.

cards.title: Vestigial
body: Leftovers — appendix, ear-wiggle muscles. Evolution’s attic.

cards.title: Criticisms of Darwin listed in the textbook
body:
1. He could not explain the *source* of variation (“survival of the fittest but not arrival of the fittest”).
2. He did not separate phenotypic from genotypic variation.
3. He thought favourable variation of both kinds was inherited.

cards.title: 2.1.4 Neo-Darwinism (synthetic theory)
body: Natural selection + Mendelian genetics + mutation (Hugo de Vries) + population genetics + isolating mechanisms + later, DNA. Variation that matters is genetic: gene and chromosome mutations. Phenotypic, environmentally acquired traits die with the individual.

steps.text: **Given:** Descriptions of origin of life concepts.
**Formula/Rule:**
- **Creationist Theory:** Assumes supernatural divine creation where all species were created simultaneously and remain immutable (unchanged).
- **Lamarckian/Darwinian Theories:** Propose organic evolution where species change gradually over time.
**Result:** The **Creationist Theory** is the correct concept.

cards.title: 2.2 Evidence for evolution · 2.2.1 Palaeontology
body: Fossils in dated rock layers show simpler forms in older strata and more complex / modern forms in younger strata. Radioactive dating (e.g. potassium–argon) gives ages of rocks and therefore of fossils.

cards.title: 2.2.1 Evidence from Paleontology
body: Palaeontology deals with the study of fossil remains of organisms or their traces.
Fossils are remains of ancestral forms that were accidentally preserved in some naturally occurring material e.g. sedimentary rock, plant resin, etc.
Palaeontology gives direct evidence that organisms living in the past were different from the organisms that are living today.
Many fossils are quite different from the forms found today, showing that evolution has taken place.

cards.title: 2.2.2 Comparative anatomy
body:
- **Homologous organs** — same underlying structure, different functions (forelimbs of human, bat, whale, horse). Suggest common ancestry.
- **Analogous organs** — same function, different structure (insect wing vs bird wing). Suggest similar selection, not close kinship.
- **Vestigial organs** — reduced leftovers (human appendix, muscles that move the ear, whale pelvic remnants).

cards.title: 2.2.2 Evidence from Comparative Anatomy
body: Comparative anatomy is the study of similarities and differences in the anatomy of organisms.
Two major concepts of comparative anatomy are: homologous organs and analogous organs.
Homologous organs are those structures which essentially have the same structure, inherited from a common ancestor, though they may be differently modified in adaptation to different functions.
An example is the forelimb structure shared by vertebrates (animals that have internal skeletons).

cards.title: 2.2.3 Biochemistry and physiology
body: All life shares DNA/RNA, ATP, similar enzymes and amino acids. The more similar the proteins or DNA sequences, the closer the relationship (e.g. human and ape haemoglobin / cytochrome).

cards.title: 2.2.3 Evidence from Biochemistry and Physiology
body: The similarities between different animals, in terms of their physiology and chemical composition, are considered to be evidence of a relationship, which shows that they have descended from a common ancestor.
The protoplasm in all organisms is the same in composition.
The nucleic acids found in chromosomes with other basic proteins are also similar in all organisms.
In the same way, very similar enzymes and hormones are found in large groups of animals.

cards.title: 2.2.4 Comparative embryology
body: Vertebrate embryos look strikingly alike early on (gill slits, tail), then diverge — interpreted as development recapping shared ancestry.

cards.title: 2.2.4 Evidence from Comparative Embryology
body: Embryology is a science which concerns the development of the embryo from the fertilization of the ovum to the fetus stage.
Embryology also provides evidence for the theory of evolution.
For example multicellular animals begin their life as a single cell (comparable to protozoa) and by repeated division, produce the blastula, which is followed by the formation of the gastrula.
In a few multi-celled animals, the embryo hatches either just after or just before the gastrula.

cards.title: 2.2.5 Geographical distribution
body: Related species on neighbouring lands or islands (Darwin’s finches) are explained by dispersal then local adaptation. Similar climates on different continents have similar-looking but unrelated organisms (convergent evolution) if the faunas were isolated.

cards.title: 2.2.5 Evidence from Geographical Distribution
body: The theory of continental drift supposes that at some time the present-day continents formed one single land mass.
Animals migrated freely across this land mass.
The land later broke up into parts, which drifted from one another forming the present-day continents.
For example in the Amazon forest, the cat family is represented by the panther and jaguar, but in Africa by the leopard, cheetah and lion.

cards.title: 2.3 Sources of genetic variation
head: Source
What the textbook emphasises
rows: Ultimate source of new alleles; gene and chromosome changes.
Whole extra chromosome sets; common in plants; can produce instant new species.
Migration of individuals / gametes moves alleles between populations.
Crossing over + independent assortment + random fertilisation shuffle existing alleles into new combinations every generation.
Stops gene flow so differences can accumulate → speciation.
Small inherited changes that improve fit to the environment, produced by selection on variation.

cards.title: 2.3 Sources of genetic variation
body: **Speciation** often begins with **geographic isolation** (mountains, rivers, deserts). After long separation, **genetic isolation** may follow so the groups cannot interbreed even if they meet again.
Other isolating mechanisms in the book: habitat, mechanical/anatomical, behavioural, seasonal, gametic mortality, zygotic mortality, hybrid inviability or sterility.

cards.title: 2.3.1 Mutation
body: An organism’s DNA affects appearance, behaviour and physiology i.e. all the aspects of life.
Mutations can be beneficial, neutral or harmful for the organism, but do not “attempt” to supply what the organism “needs”.
Mutations which cause visible changes in the chromosomes are called chromosomal mutations, or chromosomal aberrations.
Genes consist of molecules of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA).

cards.title: 2.3.2 Polyploidy
body: Diploid (2n) is the normal state, but some plants and animals are triploid (3n) or tetraploid (4n).
Polyploidy occurs due to non-disjunction i.e. an accident during meiosis or gamete formation in which homologous chromosomes fail to separate.
The tetraploids (4n) formed can mate but cannot successfully interbreed with diploid (2n) individuals from the original population.
Polyploidy seems to have been important in the evolution of plants and has probably been important as a method of genetic variation.

cards.title: 2.3.3 Gene Flow
body: Gene flow includes many different kinds of events, such as pollen being blown to a new destination or people moving to new cities or countries.

cards.title: 2.3.4 Genetic Recombination
body: In sexual reproduction, new gene combinations are introduced into a population by the shuffling of genes.
During meiosis, paternal and maternal chromosomes are reshuffled and new chromosome combinations occur.
Because gametes produced by meiosis are haploid, sexual reproduction is necessary to reconstitute the diploid genome.

cards.title: 2.3.5 Isolation
body: Without the exchange of genes, the populations tend to become progressively different from one another.
Eventually, they cannot interbreed even if brought back together.
Behavioural isolation: Behaviour may have changed so much that mating is prevented.

cards.title: 2.3.6 Adaptation
body: The processes of adaptation involve small evolutionary changes brought about by the interaction of variation and selection.
Selection operates on the available variation to produce an efficient gene pool in a particular environment.
Natural selection sorts certain gene combinations and selects others that occurred due to mutation or recombination.
Adaptation is therefore involved in producing new populations from pre-existing ones.

tips.text: The theory of evolution assumes that the present complex animals and plants have been produced in the course of thousands of years, by a process of gradual change in earlier, simpler forms of life.

Darwin’s theory can be summarized as follows: Populations tend to overproduce. They produce more offspring than are likely to survive.
The members of a population are not identical. They show variation from one to another, and these variations are inherited.

cards.title: 3.1 What is Ecology?
body: Ecology comes from the Greek words “oikos” (“house” or “place where one lives”) and “logos” (“study of”).
Ecology then means the study of the “house” in which organisms live.
An understanding of ecology is essential for the survival of humankind.

Understanding the structure and function of the various levels of ecological hierarchies and the relationships between them is vitally important for the well-being of humanity and for life in general.
Ecology is also a science that contributes considerably to the understanding of evolution.

cards.title: 3.1 What is ecology?
body: **Ecology** is the study of relationships among organisms and between organisms and their environment.

- **Species** — organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring.
- **Population** — members of one species in one area.
- **Community** — all populations interacting in an area.
- **Ecosystem** — community + abiotic environment.
- **Habitat** — the physical place a species lives.
- **Niche** — its role (what it eats, when, where, how it affects others).
- **Biosphere** — all ecosystems on Earth.
- **Biome** — a group of ecosystems with similar climate and dominant communities.

**Abiotic factors:** water, soil, pH, salinity, N and P, temperature, light, natural disasters. **Biotic factors:** all living influences (predation, competition, disease, human action such as deforestation).
Population growth depends on birth rate and death rate; most populations can grow exponentially while resources last.

steps.text: **Given:** Definitions of ecological spatial terms.
**Formula/Rule:**
- **Habitat:** The physical location or address where an organism lives (e.g., forest floor).
- **Niche:** The functional role or job of an organism in its ecosystem.
**Result:** The physical place is called the **Habitat**.

**Formula/Rule:** The correct hierarchy from smallest (least complex) to largest (most complex) is:

**Result:** The correct sequence is **Organism, Population, Community, Ecosystem, Biome**.

cards.title: 3.2 Natural cycles
body: Atoms are reused. Learn the path and the key processes, not every arrow.

cards.title: Carbon cycle
body: CO₂ in air → photosynthesis into organic carbon → food chains → respiration returns CO₂. Combustion of fossil fuels and wood adds extra CO₂. Decomposition and the ocean are major stores/exchanges.

cards.title: Oxygen cycle
body: Photosynthesis releases O₂; respiration and combustion consume it. Tightly linked to the carbon cycle.

cards.title: Nitrogen cycle
body: Air is ~78% N₂, unusable by most organisms. **Nitrogen fixation** (bacteria, some cyanobacteria; also lightning) makes ammonia. Nitrifying bacteria make nitrites then nitrates that plants absorb. Animals eat plants. Denitrifying bacteria return N₂ to air. Decomposition / ammonification recycle organic N.

cards.title: Water cycle
body: Evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, runoff, infiltration. Driven by the sun.

cards.title: 3.2 Natural cycles
body: **Phosphorus cycle** has no major atmospheric gas stage. Phosphate weathers from rock into soil and water, is taken up by producers, moves through food chains, and returns via decomposition and sedimentation. Often a limiting nutrient; excess from fertiliser causes water pollution.

cards.title: Carbon–oxygen handshake: in photosynthesis plants take in CO₂ and give out O₂; respiration (in animals, and in plants too, especially at night) does the reverse.
Mnemonic — Fix Nitrify Assimilate Denitrify
body: Nitrogen: bacteria *fix* N₂ → ammonia; others *nitrify* to nitrite then nitrate; plants *assimilate* nitrate; other bacteria *denitrify* back to N₂.
Phosphorus is the “rock cycle nutrient” — almost no air stage. If a question says “no gaseous phase”, pick phosphorus.

cards.title: 3.3 Food relationships
body: **Producers** (autotrophs, mainly photosynthesising plants and algae) convert inorganic carbon to food. **Consumers** (heterotrophs): primary (herbivores), secondary, tertiary. **Decomposers** (bacteria, fungi) recycle nutrients.
A **food chain** is one linear feeding path, e.g.
grass → grasshopper → lizard → hawk
A **food web** is the interlinked set of chains in a community — more realistic, more stable.

cards.title: 3.3 Food relationships
head: Relationship
Who benefits?
Textbook idea
rows: Parasite lives on or in a host and harms it (tapeworm, ticks, some fungi).
One benefits, the other is unaffected (e.g. epiphytes on trees).
Both benefit (N-fixing bacteria in roots; lichens; cleaner fish).
Predator kills and eats prey; important population control.

cards.title: Food chain and the direction of energy flow
body: The arrow in a food chain always shows the direction of energy flow. Each organism uses some energy, so there is less for the next level; most food chains have fewer than five links. Decomposers are placed at the end.

cards.title: 3.3.1 Food Chains
body: As energy is transferred along the chain, each organism uses some of it.
Producers have more energy available to them than consumers, thus, they are usually numerous in number.
The loss of energy along the food chain also limits its length.
For example a green plant is eaten by a herbivore and the herbivore is eaten by a carnivore.

cards.title: 3.3.2 Food Webs
body: In a community where organisms live and interact, simple food chains rarely exist, because most often the same food resource is part of more than one chain.
A food web is composed of several interconnecting food chains.
Grass is eaten by grasshoppers, which are in turn eaten by a chicken.
In the second example grass is eaten by a sheep and the sheep could then be consumed by a leopard or hyena.

cards.title: 3.3.3 Parasitism
body: Parasitism is a symbiotic relationship in which an organism obtains nutrients from another living organism without killing it.
A parasite benefits in terms of food and shelter, whereas the host is harmed in some way.
Parasites found inside the body of the host are known as endo-parasites e.g. tapeworm, Plasmodium sp., etc., whereas those parasites found on the surface of a host are called ectoparasites e.g. tick.
Natural selection favours parasites that are best able to locate and feed on the host.

cards.title: 3.3.4 Commensalism
body: Few absolute examples exist since it is unusual for one organism not to be affected in some way by a close association with another organism.
Commensalism is, however, observed in tree-roosting birds.
The trees gain nothing in return, but are not harmed by the interaction.
The remoras swim alongside the shark as it moves through the water.

cards.title: 3.3.5 Mutualism
body: A change in either organism is likely to affect the survival and reproduction of the other.
Mutualistic relationships occurs among symbiotic bacteria, such as Rhizobium bacteria in the root nodules of leguminous plants (e.g. beans or peas).
Rhizobium spp. are bacteria capable of fixing atmospheric nitrogen, which is changed into nitrates.
Plants absorb nitrates from the soil and use them for producing food, like proteins, carbohydrates and lipids.

cards.title: 3.3.6 Predation
body: The prey constitutes an organism that is hunted and killed by the predator.
Predation can occur between a hyena and a goat.
Nevertheless, some herbivores, like bark beetles, eat plant parts and often harm the plant without killing it.
Predators have a number of adaptive characteristics which make them efficient in capturing their prey.

cards.title: 3.4 Ecological pyramids
body:
- **Pyramid of numbers** — count of organisms at each trophic level. Usually upright; can invert (one tree feeding many insects).
- **Pyramid of biomass** — dry mass at each level. Usually upright on land; can invert in some oceans (phytoplankton reproduce so fast that a small standing crop supports more zooplankton).
- **Pyramid of energy** — energy flow per unit time. *Always* upright because energy is lost as heat at each transfer (~10% rule is the useful exam figure).

cards.title: Pyramid of energy
body: Producers form the large base. Energy is lost at each transfer, so each higher trophic level has less. That is why the pyramid of energy is always upright, while pyramids of numbers and biomass can be inverted.

cards.title: Energy pyramid — always a triangle pointing up. Only ~10% of energy climbs each step.
Mnemonic — +/− relationships
body: Parasite = unwelcome housemate (− host). Commensal = hitchhiker (0 host). Mutual = teammates (+ +). Predator = hunter (+ / − but prey dies).
Numbers and biomass pyramids can stand on their heads. Energy never does — heat leaks out.

cards.title: 3.4.1 Pyramids of Numbers
body: The same is done for the next step of primary producers, and so on.
When pyramids of numbers are drawn to scale, the food relationships produce a pyramid-shaped histogram called the pyramid of numbers.
The size of each block in the pyramid represents the numbers of organisms feeding at that level.
The pyramid-shaped histogram indicates a decrease in the amount of energy and number of organisms as it goes up through the trophic levels.

cards.title: 3.4.2 Pyramids of Biomass
body: The biomass of an organism is its constant total dry weight in the ecosystem.
Biomass is expressed in terms of grams per square metre (g/m2) or in metric tons (t) per hectare (ha) of material.
The shape of the pyramid narrows sharply from producers at the base to carnivores at the apex.
The producers have, then, the highest biomass per unit of area and, in decreasing order, are followed by primary-, secondary-, tertiaryand quaternary consumers.

cards.title: 3.4.3 Pyramids of Energy
body: The size of the boxes (blocks) represents the quantity of energy in the organisms.
Pyramids of energy are based on the amount of energy produced per unit area (often per square centimetre) by different tropic levels over a given period of time (typically per annum).
Pyramids of energy give a more accurate picture of the decreasing amounts of energy flowing through successive trophic levels of an ecosystem.
The rate of production of primary producers is termed “primary productivity”.

cards.title: 3.5 Biomes of the World
body: An ecosystem is a complete, life-supporting environment.
Ecosystems can be grouped according to their similarities into major ecosystems called biomes.
The major biomes of the world are classified as terrestrial and aquatic biomes.
The terrestrial biomes vary according to the type of vegetation, the climate or the dominant organisms that inhabit them.
Tropical rain forest: Tropical rain forests are located in the equatorial belt.

cards.title: 3.5 Biomes of the world
body: A biome is recognised mainly by climate and dominant vegetation.

body: Marine systems in the syllabus include the Red Sea (coral reefs). Open-ocean producers are mainly single-celled phytoplankton.

cards.title: Exam map for Eritrea
body: Present: desert, grassland/savanna. Not present: taiga, tundra. Tropical rainforest exists in Africa but is not a major Eritrean biome in the review items.
**Hottest days + coldest nights = desert.** Highest rain = tropical rainforest. Permafrost = tundra. Conifers + long winter = taiga.

cards.title: 3.6 Natural resources and survival
body: **Renewable resources** can be replaced on a human timescale if used carefully: air, water, forests, solar energy, living wildlife. **Non-renewable resources** exist in finite stocks formed over geological time: coal, oil, natural gas, most minerals.

**Pollution** is the release of harmful wastes into the environment — air (SO₂ → acid rain; smoke), water (sewage, fertiliser, oil), soil, noise, and damage to the **ozone layer** that screens UV radiation. Acid rain corrodes metals, damages buildings and can kill fish; ozone thinning is a separate problem (UV), not caused by acid rain.
**Conservation** is protection and wise use: reforestation (opposite of deforestation), wildlife reserves, sustainable harvesting, reducing emissions, protecting the ozone layer.

cards.title: 3.6.1 Types of Natural Resources
body: Renewable resources are those resources that are mainly living things, together with their products.
Non-renewable resources are those that are non-living e.g. rocks, minerals and the products of things that were once alive, like coal and petroleum.
Humans are constantly modifying their biological environment to satisfy their needs.
Other serious problems concerning humankind’s impact on the environment include pollution, deforestation and erosion.

cards.title: 3.6.2 Pollution
body: Any agent which causes pollution is called a pollutant.
The types of pollutant and their effects have greatly increased in modern times because of urbanization, overpopulation and the development of industries.
Air pollution: The harmful effects of many air pollutants are considerable.
The poisonous gases that pollute the air are sulphur dioxide, oxides of nitrogen, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, lead smoke, radiation and chloroflurocarbons (CFCs).

cards.title: 3.6.3 Conservation
body: If people are to continue to exist in the future, certain measures must be taken to ensure that adequate resources are available and pollution is controlled.
The objectives of conservation are to preserve existing natural resources, restore renewable resources and practice wise management of all non-renewable resources.

Although a number of conservation programs are in effect at present, such as the summer reforestation program and community-based building of terraces, much more needs to be done to conserve and protect Eritrea’s resources of soil, water, wildlife, atmosphere and minerals.
When people became aware of the fact that rich, productive soil had become scarce, conservation became a necessity.

items.text: In ecology, the ____, or natural cycle, is a pathway by which inorganic substances move through both biotic and abiotic elements of the ecosystem.
Among the major terrestrial ____ are the tropical rain forest, temperate deciduous forest, taiga, tundra, grassland, desert and life zones in mountains.
____ are the factors that affect a given ecosystem, and include all living elements.
____ is a symbiotic relationship in which an organism obtains nutrients from another living organism without killing it.
Another example of ____ is the relationship between a shark and the small remora fish.
Parasites found inside the body of the ____ are known as endo-parasites e.g. tapeworm, Plasmodium sp., etc., whereas those parasites found on the surface of a host are called ectoparasites e.g. tick.

similar.q: The Carbon Cycle involves  A) respiration.  B) photosynthesis.  C) decomposition.  D) industry by-products.  E) All of the above.
similar.a: E. All of the above. — Carbon moves from the air into organisms by photosynthesis and returns to the air by respiration, decomposition of dead organisms and combustion of fuels (including industrial emissions). Answer: E.

similar.q: Animals depend on bacteria and fungi because bacteria and fungi  A) do not perform photosynthesis.  B) recycle nutrients in dead organisms.  C) use sunlight to produce sugar.  D) provide animal habitat.  E) are parasites.
similar.a: B. recycle nutrients in dead organisms. — Bacteria and fungi are decomposers: they break down dead organisms and wastes, returning nutrients (N, P, C) to the soil and air for producers, on which animals ultimately depend. Answer: B.
